# Why RSNull Accepts Calls to Undefined Methods

`RSNull` is a shared object that explicitly represents a null **element** in a collection.
`RSNull$null` and `RSNull$instance` refer to the same instance.
Arrays, sets, and dictionaries do not accept R `NULL` as an element.
To store a null element, pass `RSNull$null` or call `robjc_wrap_null()` at the input boundary.

Handling null values can complicate data processing.
Consider a domain model stored in an R `list`.
If some elements are R `NULL`, ordinary code must check for them before calling a method.

```{r}
library(robjc)
items_usual <- list(RSString$new("a"), NULL)
length(items_usual)
for (item in items_usual)
  if (!is.null(item)) print(item$value()) else print(NULL)
```

For the shared `RSNull` instance, robjc instead returns that instance when an undefined method is called.
This behavior is inspired by sending messages to Objective-C's `nil`.
Using `RSNull`, the previous example becomes:

```{r}
items_rsnull <- RSArray$new(list(RSString$new("a"), RSNull$null))
items_rsnull$count()
for (item in items_rsnull$asList()) print(item$value())
```

## Reading Through Nested Objects

One null check is manageable when the desired value is close to the top of a domain model.
For a deeper value, checking after every access obscures the sequence of operations.

`RSNull` absorbs **calls** to undefined methods, so a call chain can continue through a null element.
This is useful when parsing nested, irregular JSON or XML into domain objects.
The example below parses JSON with `jsonlite` and maps three levels to `Project`, `Owner`, and `Team` classes.

```{r}
# Each JSON project has three levels: Project -> Owner -> Team.
# owner, team, and email may be null or omitted.
json <- '{
  "projects": [{
    "name": "Atlas",
    "owner": {
      "name": "Mika",
      "team": {"name": "Platform", "email": "team@example.org"}
    }
  },
  {
    "name": "Boreal",
    "owner": null
  },
  {
    "name": "Cedar",
    "owner": {
      "name": "Ken",
      "team": null
    }
  },
  {
    "name": "Delta",
    "owner": {
      "name": "Rin",
      "team": {"name": "Research"}
    }
  }]
}'
data <- jsonlite::fromJSON(json, simplifyVector = FALSE)

Team <- RSObjectClass("RSNullGuideTeam",
  private = list(.email = NULL),
  public = list(
    initialize = function(data) {
      super$initialize()
      private$.email <- if (is.null(data$email)) RSNull$null else RSString$new(data$email)
      invisible(self)
    },
    email = function() private$.email
  )
)

Owner <- RSObjectClass("RSNullGuideOwner",
  private = list(.team = NULL),
  public = list(
    initialize = function(data) {
      super$initialize()
      private$.team <- if (is.null(data$team)) RSNull$null else Team$new(data$team)
      invisible(self)
    },
    team = function() private$.team
  )
)

Project <- RSObjectClass("RSNullGuideProject",
  private = list(.name = NULL, .owner = NULL),
  public = list(
    initialize = function(data) {
      super$initialize()
      private$.name <- RSString$new(data$name)
      private$.owner <- if (is.null(data$owner)) RSNull$null else Owner$new(data$owner)
      invisible(self)
    },
    name = function() private$.name,
    owner = function() private$.owner
  )
)

projects <- RSArray$new(lapply(data$projects, function(x) Project$new(x)))
emails <- lapply(projects$asList(), function(project) project$owner()$team()$email())

stopifnot(identical(emails[[1L]]$value(), "team@example.org"))
stopifnot(all(vapply(emails[-1L], identical, logical(1), RSNull$null)))
```

JSON `null` values and omitted fields become R `NULL` after parsing.
Each class explicitly converts those values to `RSNull` in `initialize()` before storing them in the domain object.
The `projects` array contains only `Project` instances; missing values deeper in the model propagate as `RSNull`.
The result is checked for `RSNull` where that distinction matters.

### Keeping R `NULL` and Adding Guards

The next version reads the same JSON into a separate domain model that keeps missing values as R `NULL`.
It stores the model in an R `list`.
After reading each level, it must call `is.null()` before invoking another method.

```{r}
RawTeam <- RSObjectClass("RSNullGuideRawTeam",
  private = list(.email = NULL),
  public = list(
    initialize = function(data) {
      super$initialize()
      private$.email <- if (is.null(data$email)) NULL else RSString$new(data$email)
      invisible(self)
    },
    email = function() private$.email
  )
)

RawOwner <- RSObjectClass("RSNullGuideRawOwner",
  private = list(.team = NULL),
  public = list(
    initialize = function(data) {
      super$initialize()
      private$.team <- if (is.null(data$team)) NULL else RawTeam$new(data$team)
      invisible(self)
    },
    team = function() private$.team
  )
)

RawProject <- RSObjectClass("RSNullGuideRawProject",
  private = list(.name = NULL, .owner = NULL),
  public = list(
    initialize = function(data) {
      super$initialize()
      private$.name <- RSString$new(data$name)
      private$.owner <- if (is.null(data$owner)) NULL else RawOwner$new(data$owner)
      invisible(self)
    },
    name = function() private$.name,
    owner = function() private$.owner
  )
)

raw_projects <- lapply(data$projects, function(x) RawProject$new(x))
guarded_emails <- lapply(
  raw_projects,
  function(project) {
    owner <- project$owner()
    if (is.null(owner)) return(NULL)
    team <- owner$team()
    if (is.null(team)) return(NULL)
    team$email()
  }
)

stopifnot(identical(guarded_emails[[1L]]$value(), "team@example.org"))
stopifnot(all(vapply(guarded_emails[-1L], is.null, logical(1))))
stopifnot(identical(
  lapply(emails, function(x) if (identical(x, RSNull$null)) NULL else x$value()),
  lapply(guarded_emails, function(x) if (is.null(x)) NULL else x$value())
))
```

Both versions extract the same email address from the same JSON.
The `RSNull` version can express the access as one call chain; the version that retains R `NULL` needs guards after reading `owner` and `team`.
The resulting `emails` list represents missing values with `RSNull$null`, while `guarded_emails` uses R `NULL`.

This behavior has a cost: calls to undefined methods can let `RSNull` flow into a final result without an error.
Check for `RSNull` at points where the result must contain a real value.

## Distinguishing RSNull from R NULL

The behavior does not apply to the R `NULL` returned when a dictionary or set lookup finds no item.
An out-of-bounds array access raises an error.

A missing dictionary key returns R `NULL`, which remains distinguishable from a stored `RSNull`.
If processing should continue through a missing lookup result, explicitly convert it with `robjc_wrap_null()` at that boundary.

```{r}
profile <- RSMutableDictionary$new()
name_key <- RSString$new("name")
profile$setObjectForKey(RSNull$null, name_key)
missing <- profile$objectForKey(RSString$new("unknown"))
stopifnot(is.null(missing))
stopifnot(identical(profile$objectForKey(name_key), RSNull$null))

wrapped <- robjc_wrap_null(missing)
stopifnot(identical(wrapped, RSNull$null))
stopifnot(identical(wrapped$objectForKey(name_key), RSNull$null))
```

Converting every lookup result automatically would erase the distinction between an absent key and a stored `RSNull`.
Convert only where the application needs that behavior.

## Implementation: S3 `$` Dispatch

This note (05) traces why `RSNull$null$notImplementedMethod()` returns
`RSNull$null` through S3 `$` dispatch.
`RSNull` is an environment-based R6 object, and its instance also has the S3 class `RSNull`.
This lets `$.RSNull` handle `$` access.
The implementation in `R/RSNull.r` is:

```{r eval=FALSE}
`$.RSNull` <- function(x, name) {
  if (exists(name, envir = x, inherits = FALSE))
    return(get(name, envir = x, inherits = FALSE))
  function(...) RSNull$null
}
```

The method first checks for an existing binding on instance `x`.
If it finds one, it returns the original method or value, preserving the behavior of `value()`, `hash()`, and `description()`.
Otherwise, it returns a function that accepts any arguments. **Calling** that function returns `RSNull$null`.
The `inherits = FALSE` argument limits `exists()` and `get()` to bindings on the instance itself.

In `RSNull$null$notImplementedMethod()`, the first `RSNull$null` retrieves the shared instance from the generator's `null` binding.
The next `$notImplementedMethod` accesses that instance, invoking the S3 `$.RSNull` method.
Because the instance has no such binding, `$.RSNull` returns a function.
The final `()` calls that function and returns `RSNull$null`.

```{r}
fallback <- RSNull$null$notImplementedMethod
stopifnot(is.function(fallback))
stopifnot(identical(fallback(), RSNull$null))
stopifnot(identical(RSNull$null$notImplementedMethod(), RSNull$null))
```

```{r}
stopifnot(is.null(RSNull$null$value()))
stopifnot(identical(RSNull$null$unknownMethod(1, option = TRUE), RSNull$instance))
stopifnot(identical(RSNull$null$unknownMethod()$nextMethod(), RSNull$instance))
```

Merely **accessing** an undefined name with `$` does not return `RSNull`.
The lookup returns a function; calling it returns `RSNull$null`.

```{r}
stopifnot(is.function(RSNull$null$unknownMethod))
stopifnot(!RSNull$null$respondsTo("unknownMethod"))
```

## Caveats

Because calls to undefined methods are accepted, a misspelled method name does not fail at that call site.
Use `respondsTo()` when the method must exist.
Existing methods still run normally: for example, `RSNull$null$value()` returns R `NULL`, rather than the shared instance.
Keep propagation of `RSNull` separate from extracting an underlying value.
